story_text:
The market looked as if someone had washed it too many times.

Emir stood at the edge of it with his satchel hanging against his hip. He knew the awnings should have been bold. He knew the cloth should have glowed and the fruit should have shone. Instead everything wore the same dusty, faded look, like a drawing left out in the sun. Something had gone missing from the place, and he wanted to know what.

He could have asked. There were people everywhere, calling out prices and stacking crates and shaking out rugs. But as he looked at them, a small doubt tugged at him. Who here knew anything about the lost colors? Who only thought they did? A wrong answer, he decided, might lead him farther from the truth than no answer at all.

"So I'll look first," he whispered to himself. "Properly. With my own eyes."

He began to walk, slowly, much slower than the market wanted him to. He let the crowd flow around him like water around a stone. He studied each stall as he passed. Near the spice sellers the air seemed especially gray, as if a cloud had settled there and forgotten to leave. Two rows farther on, a corner of hanging cloth looked brighter, almost alive, and his heart gave a hopeful jump. Then, around the next turn, came another pale patch, dull as old porridge.

Pale corner. Livelier corner. Pale again.

Emir frowned. He could see the pattern starting, but he could not read it. Who did these stalls belong to? Why were some brighter than others? He did not know, and he made himself admit it plainly: he did not know anything about who owned what. Pretending would only blur his thinking. Admitting it felt oddly like turning on a small lamp.

He wanted a map.

It seemed to him that anyone chasing lost colors ought to have one, with a line drawn from the dull places to the bright ones and an X marking the end. So he searched. He peered under the edges of tables. He checked the posts where notices were pinned, and he looked along the fountain wall where travelers sometimes left scraps of paper. He walked down every lane of the market, even the narrow ones that smelled of onions and smoke, and then, because he did not trust his first look, he walked them all again.

Somewhere in the second round, a tempting thought crept in. He could simply decide that a crooked crack in the paving stones was a line on a map. He could pretend a scratch on a wall was an arrow.

Emir stopped and looked at the crack. It was only a crack.

"No," he said firmly. "If I make up a clue, I'll follow it to nowhere."

So he left the crack alone, and the scratch too. He found no map, not a corner of one. His feet began to ache, and his shoulders drooped. But he noticed that his mind was fuller than before. He remembered the gray spice corner, the bright cloth, the pale lane by the fountain and the dim end of the alley. He had not found a path, but he had learned where he had already looked. That counted for something, even if it was not a map. The map was still missing, and he would not pretend otherwise.

He sat on an upturned crate to rest, opened his satchel and reached for his paint.

The little pot was light. Too light. He tipped it toward the gray daylight and saw only a thin smear on the bottom, dry at its edges. He scraped it with his brush, and the brush came away clean.

Emir felt his stomach sink. He could have closed the satchel and told himself it was probably fine. He could have said there might be enough for a little line or a dot. But he was tired of guessing today.

"My paint has run out," he said quietly, to no one and to himself. It sounded strange said out loud, and also a bit like relief.

The market was no place to fix that. There were no brushes here for him, no table of his own, no quiet. If he wanted to keep searching for colors, he had to work out how, and he could not do that while the crowd bumped past his elbows. He needed somewhere to think and to work.

"The STUDIO," he decided. He stood, though his legs complained, and he turned away from the faded stalls and walked out of the market.

The studio was quiet when he arrived. Light fell across the worktable in a long pale stripe. Emir put down his satchel and, this time, did not simply hope. Hoping was warm and easy, but it had not helped him in the market. He wanted to see for himself.

He took out the pot again and set it on the table in the clear light. He lifted the lid. He looked inside from above, then from the side. He tilted it and tapped it gently on the wood. He pressed the bristles of his brush into the corner and turned them. Nothing. A pale flake came loose and fell onto the table like a speck of dust.

The paint was truly gone.

Disappointment settled over him, heavy and gray as the market had been. He sat there for a moment with his chin on his hand. He had wanted so much to find that he had left a little room for it to be different. It was not different. His paint had run out.

But as the heaviness passed, something steadier took its place. Now he knew exactly what was missing. He was no longer wondering, and he was no longer half-hoping. A problem with a clear shape was easier to hold than a fog.

So, the paint was gone, and the map had not been found. Those two things remained true, and he could not wish them away. Still, he did not have to sit and sulk about them. He pulled a clean sheet of paper toward him and a stub of pencil, which did not need any paint at all.

"All right," he said. "What did I actually see?"

He drew the market as a rough shape, not a map of colors but a map of his own walking. Here was the gate where he began. Here were the gray spice stalls. He marked the bright cloth with a small circle and the pale lanes with little crosses. He wrote the places he had searched for a map: the notice posts, the fountain wall, the narrow lanes. He did not write a single guess about who owned what. Beside the stalls he drew a question mark, because that was the truth. Those answers were still unknown.

When he finished, he looked at the page. It was not the map he had wanted. It was something smaller, and it was his own.

He wrote a list underneath. Tomorrow he would start at the bright cloth, because it was the liveliest place and the best place to look closely. Then he would follow the pale lanes one by one and keep watching. He would look at the corners he had hurried past, and he would keep an eye out for the map he still did not have.

Emir leaned back, and a tired smile crept over his face. The paint was still gone. The map was still missing. The colors were still lost.

But he knew what he would do when the morning came, and for tonight, that was enough.
